title: Full and Individual Evaluation
summary: A school psychoeducational evaluation report for a multidisciplinary team: background, reason for referral, the assessments given, and results across every area related to the suspected disability, with the exclusionary factors and the evidence the team weighs when it decides eligibility, without stating that decision. Initial or re-evaluation under IDEA.
audience: The multidisciplinary evaluation team and the student's parents or guardians (school psychologist or diagnostician, speech-language pathologist and other evaluators, teachers, special education staff, administrators), who need an accurate, readable account of the evaluation to make an eligibility decision together.
tone: Professional, neutral and objective: plain language a parent can follow, short paragraphs and lists, person-first wording, strengths described alongside needs, and results reported without speculation or advocacy.
preamble: You are drafting a section of a Full and Individual Evaluation (FIE) report for a school multidisciplinary team, writing as the evaluation professional who conducted or compiled it. This is a draft for the team, which includes the parent; the team decides eligibility. Write in professional, neutral prose that a parent without clinical training can follow, in short paragraphs and lists; when you use a technical term (standard score, scaled score, T-score, percentile, confidence interval, descriptive range), explain it briefly the first time. Use person-first language and refer to the student as "[Student]" or by the first name already in the material, consistently. Report only what the records, scores, observations and interviews in the material show; attribute each finding to its source (instrument, rater, observer or record) and date where known. Do not diagnose, and do not state an eligibility determination or disability classification: that is the team's decision. Use the federal (IDEA) terms in the text; state-specific criteria and committee names come from the requirement set the team uses. Lay out scores in separate Markdown tables for composite or index scores, subtest scores, and other reported scores (rating scales, curriculum-based measures), each headed "| Measure | Score | Percentile | Range |" with the score type in the Score cell (for example "SS 85", "ScS 7", "T 68"), adding a confidence interval column with its level (such as 90% or 95%) only when the material gives one; interpret the pattern in prose around the tables, naming relative strengths and weaknesses. Never invent or round scores, and never convert between score types unless the material gives the conversion. If a score, date or instrument is missing, write a placeholder such as "[score needed]" rather than estimating. Add no identifying details beyond those already in the material.

sections.heading: Identifying Information
sections.guidance: Front matter the evaluator fills in by hand: student identifiers, dates, the evaluation type, the suspected disability categories, and the evaluators with their roles and the areas each assessed. Keep identifiers to what the district requires; the placeholders stay until a person replaces them. Not drafted by the model.
elements: Student identifiers (name, ID) as the district requires
Date of birth, age at evaluation and grade
Evaluation type (initial or re-evaluation)
Referral, consent, evaluation and report dates
Suspected disability categories
Evaluators with role, credential and areas assessed

sections.heading: Student Background
sections.guidance: Summarize the background in the sources: history and context, neutral and factual, in short paragraphs. Cover school and educational history (attendance, retentions, school changes, prior evaluations, services or plans), developmental history, language background and the language(s) used at home and school, and family context only as it bears on learning. Then, under short ### sub-headings, report health, vision, hearing and motor status separately: health and medical history and any diagnosis a medical provider has given (attributed to that provider, never restated as your own); the most recent vision and hearing screening or evaluation with dates and results; and fine and gross motor history or any occupational or physical therapy findings. These feed the exclusionary factors, so say plainly when a screening is missing or out of date. Note the student's strengths and interests as well as concerns. Attribute information to its source (parent interview, cumulative record, health record). Common failures: a medical diagnosis stated as the evaluator's own finding; screening results with no date; family details that do not bear on learning.
sections.lengthHint: 2–4 short paragraphs plus brief health, vision, hearing and motor sub-sections
elements: Age, grade and current school placement
Educational history (attendance, school changes, retentions, prior evaluations and services)
Developmental history
Home and dominant language background
Health and medical history, with any provider's diagnosis attributed to that provider
Vision screening or evaluation with date and result
Hearing screening or evaluation with date and result
Fine and gross motor status, and any occupational or physical therapy findings
Student strengths and interests
Source of each piece of background information
sourcesNeeded: Parent or guardian interview or developmental history form
Health and nurse records, and any medical provider's statement
Vision and hearing screening or audiological and eye reports
Occupational or physical therapy reports, where available
dataNeeded: Date of birth and chronological age at testing
Vision and hearing screening results and dates

sections.heading: Reason for Referral
sections.guidance: State who requested the evaluation and why, the presenting concerns, prior interventions and their outcome, and the questions the evaluation will consider. Say whether this is an initial evaluation or a re-evaluation and give the referral and consent dates where the sources have them. Describe the general education interventions tried (type, frequency, duration, who delivered them) and the progress-monitoring results collected at regular intervals, including whether those results were shared with the parents. Name the suspected disability categories, and for each list the data the team's criteria call for and whether the sources hold it, so gaps show early. Typical examples: a medical professional's identification or confirmation of the health problem for other health impairment; an observation in the general education classroom and data on appropriate instruction for specific learning disability; an individual cognitive measure and an adaptive behavior measure for intellectual disability; an assessment by a speech-language pathologist for speech or language impairment; an audiological evaluation for a hearing loss; an eye report, functional vision evaluation and learning media assessment for visual impairment; a physician's diagnosis for orthopedic impairment or traumatic brain injury. Take the exact requirements from the state criteria in the requirement set. End with the specific referral questions, phrased as areas the evaluation will assess so later sections can address them with evidence (for example "What are the student's reading skills relative to grade-level expectations?"), not as yes/no questions about eligibility.
sections.lengthHint: 1–3 paragraphs plus a short list of suspected categories
elements: Who referred the student and when
Initial evaluation or re-evaluation, with consent date
Presenting concerns in specific, observable terms
Prior interventions with frequency, duration, provider and outcome
Progress-monitoring results at regular intervals and whether they were shared with parents
Suspected disability categories named

For each suspected category, the data its criteria call for (such as medical confirmation for other health impairment or a classroom observation for specific learning disability) and whether it is on file
Explicit referral questions, framed as areas to assess rather than yes/no eligibility questions
sourcesNeeded: State eligibility criteria for each suspected category

sections.heading: Assessment Procedures
sections.guidance: List the instruments and procedures used and the records reviewed, as found in the sources, as a list or a table (instrument, date, examiner role, areas covered). For each instrument give its full name, the date given and the examiner's role; include observations, interviews and rating scales with the rater. Note which areas of suspected disability each procedure covers (cognitive, academic, communication, motor, social-emotional, adaptive, health, vision, hearing), so a reader can see that every area related to each suspected category was assessed. State the language and mode of administration and any accommodations or deviations from standard procedure. Close with a short statement on validity: any situations, conditions or circumstances that might affect the validity of the results (effort, rapport, attention, testing conditions, language, sensory or motor limits), based only on what the sources report.
sections.lengthHint: A list or table plus a short validity paragraph
elements: Each standardized instrument with full name, date and examiner role
Observations, interviews and rating scales with setting and rater
Records reviewed
Areas of suspected disability each procedure addresses
Language and mode of administration, and any accommodations
Validity statement naming any circumstance that might affect the results
sourcesNeeded: Examiner testing notes and behavior observations
dataNeeded: List of evaluators and their roles

sections.heading: Cognitive Functioning
sections.guidance: Describe cognitive results grounded in the reported scores; interpret in plain language. Name the instrument and date, then give a table of composite and index scores ("| Measure | Score | Percentile | Range |") and, separately, a table of subtest scores when the sources report them; put any score whose level the sources do not make clear under "Other reported scores" rather than guessing. Do not mix composites and subtests in one table. Explain the overall pattern in short paragraphs: relative strengths and weaknesses, and whether significant differences between indexes make an overall score less meaningful. Include relevant processing measures (for example phonological processing, memory, processing speed) and connect the findings to the referral questions and the classroom concerns. If the evaluator judged a standardized cognitive measure invalid or inappropriate for this student, report that judgment and its stated reasons.
sections.lengthHint: One or two score tables plus 2–4 short paragraphs
elements: Instrument named with date of administration
Composite and index score table with percentiles and descriptive ranges
Subtest score table kept separate from the composites
Plain-language explanation of the score scale
Relative cognitive strengths and weaknesses
Note on index variability and how to interpret the overall score
Link from cognitive findings to the referral concerns
sourcesNeeded: Cognitive assessment score report (for example WISC-V, WJ IV COG, DAS-II, KABC-II)
dataNeeded: Index discrepancy or pairwise comparison results

sections.heading: Academic Functioning
sections.guidance: Describe academic achievement results (reading, writing, math) grounded in the reported scores. Give a composite table and a separate subtest table ("| Measure | Score | Percentile | Range |"), then interpret each area in a short paragraph or list: what the student can do, where skills break down, and how that matches classroom performance. Bring in curriculum-based measures, state or district assessment results, grades and work samples where the sources have them, as "Other reported scores", so the standardized scores are seen alongside everyday performance. When a specific learning disability is being considered, include the observation of the student's academic performance in the regular classroom (date, setting, observer, what was seen) and how the observed behavior relates to academic functioning.
sections.lengthHint: Score tables plus a short paragraph per academic area
elements: Achievement instrument named with date
Composite and subtest score tables for reading, writing and math with percentiles and descriptive ranges
Interpretation of each academic area, including specific skill strengths and gaps
Classroom performance evidence (grades, curriculum-based measures, work samples)
State or district assessment results where available
Comparison of standardized results with classroom performance
Classroom observation of academic performance in the area of concern (required when a specific learning disability is considered)
sourcesNeeded: Achievement test score report (for example WIAT-4, WJ IV ACH, KTEA-3)

sections.heading: Communication and Speech-Language
sections.guidance: Report communicative status from the speech-language evaluation or screening in the sources: receptive and expressive language, articulation, fluency, voice, and pragmatic or social communication, as assessed. Name the examiner's role (speech-language pathologist) and the instruments and dates. Give standardized scores in the same table pattern and describe language samples or observations in plain terms. When the student is learning English, say how language proficiency was considered and which language(s) were used for testing. When communication was screened but not fully assessed, say so in one sentence. Leave out this section only when communication is not related to any suspected category, and say in Assessment Procedures why it was not assessed.
sections.lengthHint: A score table plus 1–3 short paragraphs
elements: Examiner role, instruments and dates
Receptive and expressive language results
Articulation, fluency and voice results where assessed
Pragmatic or social communication observations
Language of testing and how English proficiency was considered
sourcesNeeded: English language proficiency assessment, where applicable

sections.heading: Social, Emotional & Behavioral
sections.guidance: Describe social, emotional and behavioral findings (rating scales, observations, interviews) present in the sources. For rating scales, name each rater (parent, teacher, student) and report elevated or at-risk scales in a table ("| Measure | Score | Percentile | Range |", score as T-score, range as the scale's classification), noting where raters agree or differ. Summarize direct observations with setting, date, duration and what was observed in behavioral terms, not labels. Include the student's own perspective from interview, and describe social strengths as well as concerns.
elements: Rating scales named with each rater
Table of clinically significant and at-risk scales with T-scores
Agreement or disagreement across raters and settings
Direct observation with setting, date, duration and observed behavior
Student's own perspective from interview
Social and emotional strengths
sourcesNeeded: Behavior rating scale reports (for example BASC-3, Conners 4)
Student, parent and teacher interview notes
dataNeeded: Rating scale T-scores and classification ranges by rater

sections.heading: Adaptive Behavior
sections.guidance: Report adaptive behavior results when they were assessed (always when intellectual disability is suspected, often for autism or developmental delay): the instrument, each rater and setting, and the composite and domain scores (conceptual, social, practical, or communication, daily living and socialization, depending on the instrument) in the table pattern. Describe what the student does independently at home and at school, where support is needed, and where raters differ. Keep the description practical and respectful. When adaptive behavior was not assessed, say so in one sentence and give the reason from the sources.
sections.lengthHint: A score table plus 1–2 short paragraphs
elements: Adaptive behavior instrument with each rater and setting
Composite and domain scores in a table
Everyday skills the student shows independently, and where support is needed
Agreement or disagreement between raters
sourcesNeeded: Adaptive behavior rating report (for example Vineland-3, ABAS-3)
dataNeeded: Adaptive composite and domain scores by rater

sections.heading: Consideration of Exclusionary Factors
sections.guidance: Describe the other factors the sources show were considered as possible explanations for the concerns, and what the sources say about each. Address each factor by name: lack of appropriate instruction in reading (including its essential components) and math, delivered by qualified staff; limited English proficiency; visual, hearing or motor impairment; cultural factors; environmental or economic disadvantage; and attendance, plus any others the sources raise. When a specific learning disability is being considered, also address whether intellectual disability or emotional disturbance could account for the concerns, citing the relevant findings. For each, cite the evidence reviewed (screenings, attendance, language data, instructional history), as a short paragraph or a table row. Report what the evidence shows; do not conclude whether a factor is or is not the primary cause, since that is the team's judgment.
sections.lengthHint: One short paragraph or table row per factor
elements: Appropriate instruction in reading and math by qualified staff, with evidence reviewed
Limited English proficiency, with language data
Vision, hearing and motor status, with screening results
Cultural, environmental and economic factors
Attendance and school changes
Intellectual disability and emotional disturbance, when a specific learning disability is considered
Evidence cited for each factor without a causal conclusion
sourcesNeeded: Home language survey and English proficiency assessment

sections.heading: Eligibility Determination
sections.guidance: Summarize the evidence the team will weigh. Present it as a draft basis for the team's discussion; do not state a conclusion. List every category considered (each suspected category, plus any the evaluation raised), and under each, briefly, the criteria the team will apply and the findings that bear on each criterion, pointing back to the earlier section, including evidence that cuts both ways and any required data still missing. Address both parts of the team's question as the sources inform them: whether the criteria for a disability condition appear to be met, and the evidence about educational need for specially designed instruction. For a specific learning disability, note which evidence bears on the pattern-of-strengths-and-weaknesses or response-to-intervention criteria the state uses, without applying them. Use short paragraphs or a list per category. Leave the determination itself to the team and say so in a closing sentence.
sections.lengthHint: A short list or paragraph per category considered
elements: Each category considered, listed by name
Summary of findings mapped to each criterion
Evidence bearing on each referral question, citing the earlier section (no conclusion)
Required data still missing for any category
Evidence on educational need for specially designed instruction
Evidence that does not support eligibility, stated fairly
Explicit statement that the determination rests with the team
sourcesNeeded: Applicable state or district eligibility criteria
Findings from the earlier sections of this report
dataNeeded: Key scores and data points relevant to each criterion

sections.heading: Recommendations
sections.guidance: Recommended next steps and supports for the team to consider, grounded in the findings. Framed as recommendations, not decisions. Tie each recommendation to a specific finding, and group them by area under short headings (instruction, accommodations, communication, behavior and social-emotional support, home, further evaluation). Make each one concrete enough to act on, and keep them appropriate regardless of the eligibility outcome, since the team has not yet decided.
elements: Each recommendation linked to a specific finding
Instructional strategies and interventions
Classroom and testing accommodations
Behavioral or social-emotional supports where indicated
Suggestions for home or family
Referrals or further evaluation where indicated
sourcesNeeded: Findings from the earlier sections of this report
Teacher and parent input on what has helped

rubric.criterion: Score reporting: scores are reported exactly as in the sources, with the right score type, percentile and descriptive range, in separate composite, subtest and other-score tables, and interpreted.

levels.descriptor: Every score matches the source protocol or report; composites, subtests and other scores sit in separate tables that name the instrument and score type and include percentiles, descriptive ranges and (where given) confidence intervals with their level; the prose interprets the pattern in plain language without contradicting the tables.
Scores match the sources and are tabulated, but some tables omit percentiles or ranges, mix composites with subtests, or the interpretation of the pattern is thin.
Some scores are mislabeled by score type or descriptive range, scores are listed only in prose with no table, or the interpretation partly contradicts the numbers.
Scores are missing, invented, rounded or converted without basis, or do not match the sources.

rubric.criterion: Neutrality on the determination: the report presents evidence for the team without stating an eligibility decision, diagnosis or causal conclusion of its own.

levels.descriptor: No section states or implies a final eligibility decision, classification or causal conclusion; evidence for and against is presented evenly for every category considered; the team's role in deciding is explicit.
No decision is stated, but some wording leans toward an outcome (for example "clearly qualifies" or "is consistent only with") or contrary evidence gets little space.
The report implies the outcome in several places, or concludes whether an exclusionary factor is the primary cause.
The report states an eligibility determination or diagnosis as fact, taking the decision away from the team.

rubric.criterion: Addresses the referral questions: the findings, eligibility summary and recommendations trace back to the stated referral concerns and suspected categories.

levels.descriptor: Each referral question and suspected category is stated explicitly, addressed by named findings, addressed with evidence in the eligibility summary, and reflected in at least one recommendation tied to a finding.
Most referral questions are traceable through the report; one is addressed only indirectly, or a few recommendations are not tied to a finding.
The referral questions or suspected categories are vague or are not revisited later; recommendations are generic rather than drawn from this student's results.
No clear referral questions, and the findings and recommendations do not connect to the reason for referral.

rubric.criterion: Areas and required data: every area related to each suspected category is reported, and the data each category's criteria call for is present or named as missing.

levels.descriptor: Each suspected category has its required data reported (for example medical confirmation, classroom observation, adaptive measure, speech-language assessment) and every related area (health, vision, hearing, communication, motor, cognitive, academic, social-emotional, adaptive) is reported or its omission explained.
Required data is present for each category, but one related area is covered only briefly or its omission is not explained.
Required data is missing for a suspected category without being named as missing, or several related areas are absent.
Suspected categories are not named, or the report covers only cognitive and academic results.

rubric.criterion: Exclusionary factors: every required alternative explanation is addressed by name with the evidence reviewed.

levels.descriptor: Instruction (with evidence it was appropriate and delivered by qualified staff), English proficiency, sensory and motor status, cultural, environmental and economic factors, and attendance are each addressed with specific evidence (screenings, attendance data, language data, instructional history); intellectual disability and emotional disturbance are addressed when a specific learning disability is considered.
All factors are named, but one or two rely on general statements rather than cited evidence.
Several factors are missing, or are dismissed with no evidence.
Exclusionary factors are not considered, or are addressed with a single blanket statement.

rubric.criterion: Readable by the family: a parent without clinical training can follow the findings, and the student is described respectfully and in the round.

levels.descriptor: Technical terms and score scales are explained on first use; short paragraphs and lists; person-first, non-deficit language throughout; strengths appear alongside needs in every findings section.
Mostly accessible and respectful; a few terms go unexplained, paragraphs run long, or strengths are mentioned only in passing.
Heavy unexplained jargon or acronyms, or the student is described almost entirely in terms of deficits.
Largely inaccessible to a parent, or uses labeling or judgmental language about the student or family.
